text: How is reading the Bible like playing
with Lego bricks? Hey everybody, I'm Dan
Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and
religion. And I have a particular theory
of biblical interpretation. And I don't
really have a good name for it yet, but
I generally refer to it as the Lego
bricks theory of biblical
interpretation. And this is a metaphor
that I developed after I had a number of
people on the internet tell me that, oh,
when it comes to how to interpret a
given passage, you have to consider the
whole cannon of the Bible. You have to
look at the picture on the box to
understand how you're supposed to
interpret this one little passage. And
that argument never sat well with me
because there is no box and there is no
picture on the box.
The notion that there's a picture on the
box is really just an appeal to your
tradition. What your own tradition says
holistically the Bible is about is the
picture on the box. But what if I don't
want to understand this particular
passage through the interpretive lenses
of your particular tradition? What if I
want to understand what the biblical
authors were trying to say on their own
terms? Well, that doesn't really work
with this picture on the box idea. So, I
came up with a different metaphor for
understanding what we're doing when
we're reading the Bible. And it was
based on my experience growing up as a
kid. I lived in the basement of this
town home that we lived in in Maryland.
And we had a giant toy box that was
shaped like a football with a lid that
you popped off. And sometimes we had a
bunch of Legos in there. And so my
theory begins from the notion of a big
toy box full of Lego bricks. So this is
the Bible. Imagine there's a label
across that toy box that says the Bible.
Dump out all those Lego bricks. Each one
of those bricks is like a verse or maybe
even a clause within a verse. But the
pile of bricks you now have all over the
floor constitutes a bunch of different
sets that were intended to build
specific things. Uh some of the sets are
whole, some of the sets are pretty
fragmentaryary. They're a bunch of stray
bricks as well. Uh and basically you
just set to work trying to build
something. And in trying to build
something, you're going to fall
somewhere along a spectrum of intent
where on one end of the spectrum, you're
building whatever you want to build.
Whatever is going to be most meaningful
or useful or fun for you, that's what
you're building. So, you don't
necessarily have to use the bricks from
a given set to create what that set was
intended to build. You can use them to
build whatever you want. That's on this
end of the spectrum. On the other end of
the spectrum, maybe we want to actually
complete this set. We might not have all
the pieces, but based on what we do see,
maybe we can get most of the way towards
figuring out what was this set intended
to build. And maybe we try to build
that. We don't have the instructions. We
certainly don't have the picture on the
box, but based on our knowledge of how
LEGO works, maybe we can get most of the
way there. Maybe we can construct the
thing and be like, "Yeah, it's got some
gaps in it, but we're pretty sure we
know what it is." And maybe you bring in
some pieces from another set to complete
the picture. But that's the spectrum.
And you're going to be somewhere in
between the two ends of that spectrum.
And why is this more like the Bible than
the whole picture on the box idea? Well,
again, because we don't have a picture
on the box.
We are interpreting the Bible according
to whatever interpretive lenses we bring
to the Bible. And those interpretive
lenses are going to have rhetorical
goals. And if our rhetorical goal is to
leverage the Bible to gatekeep or to
structure power and boundaries and
values in the service of our own
identity politics or advance our own
personal interests or protect our own
personal interests within the social
identities that are important to us,
then we're going to be on this side of
the spectrum. We're going to be
constructing whatever we need to to
serve our own interests, which means
we're not even going to care what these
sets were originally intended to build.
And then if we are engaging the Bible
because we want to know what they
actually thought anciently, then we're
going to be closer to the other end of
the spectrum. We are going to be trying
to figure out where these pieces were
intended to go. We're going to try to
figure out what these sets were intended
to build. And it's going to be
frustrating because there are going to
be plenty of times when we just don't
have enough information. We don't have
all the pieces and we don't know how
they were supposed to go together. And
we can try and we can get pretty close.
Maybe we think, but it's never going to
be perfect. But that's on the other end
of the spectrum. And I think this is a
much better analogy because in the end
when people talk about things that are
biblical,
overwhelmingly they're not talking about
